author: ohtadmin
title: Famed photographer captures his home
text:
One of the best ways to experience Conanicut Island from the comfort of your own couch has just been published.
Onne van der Wal, whose nautical photography has literally taken him around the world, has released a 244-page book titled “Jamestown, Rhode Island.”
While the Dutchman is renowned for capturing regattas, including his global circumnavigation onboard Flyer II for the 1981-82 Whitbread Round the World Race, the self-published book explores a more intimate area of Earth.
Van der Wal’s 9.7-squaremile home on Narragansett Bay.
“It shows everything that Jamestown is made of,” he said.
Van der Wal, who moved to Jamestown in 1997, said he approached the coffee-table book as a labor of love, not an assignment. While he had the idea for this project in the back of his head, it wasn’t until 2023 when a solicitation arrived in the mail that inspired him to get started. The offer was from Blurb, a company that helps people publish books.
“It’s very inexpensive,” van der Wal said. “They offered to do it for free. But that’s when I decided I should do a book about Jamestown. But if I’m going to put all this effort in, it should be a proper Jamestown book. That was the turning point.”
That’s when he called his designer, Dean Bubello, to discuss how he would approach the project. He had thousands of photos. There were digital photos taken from helicopters, analog photos taken from boats. The collection, however, was missing something.
“I had tons of photos of Jamestown in the winter, spring and fall,” he said. “But I had very little from the summer. I was always shooting sailboats on the water. That was my job. I didn’t want this to be a sailing book. I wanted this to be a Jamestown book.”
A man for all seasons
Van der Wal and Bubello decided the book should be broken into seasons. Because he had so few summer photos, however, they decided it should be a combination of his archives and yet-to-be-taken photographs, which is how he spent the last two years. The photos range from the Jamestown Windmill 35 years ago to a group photograph of the fire department in May.
“The whole experience of shooting Jamestown was amazing because I was able to explore every nook and cranny,” he said. “It was just a really great time getting to know the rock.”
An unexpected barrier, however, emerged when van der Wal was diagnosed with pancreatic cancer shortly after the Blurb offer arrived. While his project started slowly as he underwent chemotherapy, he gradually started to feel better following Whipple surgery to remove part of his pancreas.
“I began swimming again and little by little I was getting my strength back,” he said. “And I did it on my own. I never went with anyone else. I didn’t want someone to say, ‘I’m hungry. Let’s go.’ Because if I’m hungry, I don’t care. If I can see the clouds are going to be clear in a half hour, I’ll sit and wait. It’s going to be spectacular. I’ll read my iPhone. Listen to the birds. Smell nature. I did many, many, many mornings and afternoons like that. It’s hard to explain that experience. But I can see it in this book.”
More than landscapes and seascapes, lighthouses and sailboats, forts and farms, van der Wal wanted to capture the community. That meant meeting the people who shaped it. He baked bread with Andrea Colognese, designed shoes with Martin Keen, petted cows with Chandler Neale, sculpted with Peter Diepenbrock, shellfished with Mark Goerner.
“We spent a morning on his boat collecting oysters,” van der Wal said. “You can hear the seagulls and smell the ocean. I’m out there with the earlymorning light shining on the Dutch Island Lighthouse as we are pulling up cages. What an incredible time.”
Van der Wal credited James Wright, who wrote the foreword, for serving as the middleman when it came to getting access, which led to photographs from sites like Horsehead, Fox Hill Farm, Clingstone and Watson Farm.
“The manager of the farm, Max Sherman, showed me all around in his truck,” he said. “And he told me, ‘Come back anytime. Drive where you like. Just let me know when you’re coming and when you’re leaving.’ I’d come to visit the sheep at sunrise or late in the day. Whenever I was there, something was interesting. I went back four or five times. I got so much beautiful stuff. And these people became my mates. They were so supportive. Every door opened. There were people who I thought I knew much better and people who I didn’t know at all. They really got to the nittygritty of Jamestown.”
No place like home
One of the most nostalgic memories in the book is captured by a four-shot package of the Jamestown Bridge being demolished.
“That was an epic event for all of us living here at that time,” he said. “Boom, boom, boom, as it all came down. It happened so quickly.”
Along with Wright and Bubello, van der Wal commended his wife, Tenley, who had the final say on which photos made the final cut, how they were cropped and where they went.
“She got involved during the second half of the project,” he said. “I could not have done it without her.”
Van der Wal said “working in his backyard” was essential to completing a project like this.
“I’ve traveled to Australia, New Zealand, South Africa and the Caribbean,” he said. “I’ve been all around the world. It’s beautiful, but it’s exhausting. There are weird languages. Weird food. To have an assignment like this in my backyard, it’s a treat. Especially a place as beautiful as Jamestown. It’s great just to be able to go back to the same place three times if I need to. I can look out of my bedroom window, see the sky, grab a cup of tea and be where I need to be in six minutes.”
While a slideshow of the photographs that appear in the book was shown during a private event at the Jamestown Arts Center, and he signed books during a party at Riven Rock, van der Wal is eager for the rest of the community to see his final product.
While the photos capture the beauty of Jamestown, he said, the captions accompanying them capture the community.
“I really dug deep to put this together,” he said. “It’s a love letter to a place like no other.”
Get the book
“Jamestown, Rhode Island,” by Onne van der Wal, is available at Fuller Gallery, 42 Narragansett Ave., and TWC Home, 17 Narragansett Ave. It also can be purchased at his gallery in Newport, 1 Bannister’s Wharf, and at his website, vanderwal.com.
